turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's nice to meet you too, Dr. Smith. I, um, I came in today because things have just gotten to a point where I really don't know what else to do with myself. I mean, at my age—I'm 66 now, you know, and I haven't been working for a while—people always tell you that you should be relaxing, taking it easy, enjoying the quiet time, or whatever it is folks my age are supposed to do. But I just... I feel like I absolutely cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. 

It's this constant, awful buzzing feeling, if that makes any sense. I'll be sitting in my living room, maybe trying to watch a program, and I know I should just be sitting still because I am so completely worn out. I mean, bone-tired. But my body just won't listen. It's like I have to jump up and do the next thing, and then the next thing, even if there isn't really a 'next thing' that actually needs doing. I'll just suddenly be on my feet, walking into the kitchen or fussing with something on the counter, and it's just exhausting. I want to rest, I really truly do, but this feeling inside me just won't let me just sit in a chair and be. It's driving me absolutely up the wall.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an inability to settle, a constant buzzing feeling, and the urge to jump up and do things even when trying to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient explicitly states feeling 'completely worn out,' 'bone-tired,' and finds their restlessness 'exhausting.'

turns.doctor_question: When you feel this urge to move, is it because you are feeling anxious and worried about something, or is it purely a physical sensation that you just need to move your legs or body?
turns.patient_response:
Well, gosh, you know, I’m really not entirely sure how to answer that. I mean, I’ve actually sat and tried to figure that out myself, because my sister is always telling me, "What are you so anxious about?" But I don't... I don't really know if it's a worry. I mean, I don't think I'm sitting there fretting over the grocery bills or the state of the world or anything like that when it happens. But then again, maybe I am? It’s just so hard to untangle it all. 

It mostly just feels like this... this intense physical pressure, mostly in my legs. Like a motor running right under my skin. I’ll be in my recliner—it's this lovely brown one I bought when I finally stopped working, thinking I’d be spending all this time reading all those books I never had time for—and I just get this creeping sensation. I honestly don't know if my mind starts it or if my body starts it, to be perfectly honest with you. I just know that suddenly my body says "go." And I'll try to tell myself, "Now listen here, just stay put, you're exhausted, there's absolutely nothing that needs doing," but it doesn't do a lick of good. 

So I can't say for sure if there's some hidden anxious thought causing it, or if it's purely just my body needing to move... I just know I end up up on my feet, pacing around the kitchen island or wiping down a counter that's already perfectly clean, for absolutely no earthly reason, just wearing out the soles of my slippers. It's just so frustrating because I really do want to just sit, but I can't quite tell what's driving me out of the chair in the first place.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes being unable to stay seated in her recliner, stating she ends up on her feet pacing around.

turns.doctor_question: Does this sensation in your legs become more intense or noticeable when you are trying to wind down in the evening or when you are lying in bed at night?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, I’ve heard people talk about that—my neighbor, Shirley, she says she gets the jimmy legs right when she gets under the covers, where she just kicks and kicks all night. But for me? No, I really wouldn't say it's an evening thing or a nighttime thing specifically. Not at all. I mean, I could be sitting at the kitchen table at ten o'clock in the morning, trying to drink my decaf—I actually switched to decaf a few months back because my sister said, "Maybe it's the coffee making you so jumpy," but I'll tell you what, it didn't make a lick of difference—and I'll get that exact same feeling. It doesn't matter if the sun is coming up or if it's pitch black outside. 

Like just yesterday, I was trying to sit and sort through some old mail right after lunch, broad daylight, just trying to make a pile for recycling and a pile for bills, and I just couldn't stay in the chair. I had to get up and walk around the house three times before I could even look at the next envelope. So when I lay down in bed at night, sure, I might feel it then too, because I'm trying to lay down and go to sleep, but it's definitely not any worse or more intense than it is at two in the afternoon. 

It's just... it's all the time. If I'm awake, and I'm trying to be still, that motor is running. I try to read my magazines, I get the Good Housekeeping and the Reader's Digest, and I can't even get through a simple recipe for a casserole without my legs deciding they need to be in the hallway. So, no, I don't think it's tied to bedtime or winding down at all. It's just tied to me trying to sit still, period, no matter what time the clock on the wall says.

turns.doctor_question: Are you currently taking any prescription medications for your physical or mental health, or have you recently started or changed any medications?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, not really. I mean, I don't take anything at all right now, not for my mind or my body. I know folks my age usually have a whole pillbox sitting on the kitchen counter—my sister, she has one of those plastic ones with the days of the week on it, morning and night, and she’s always snapping those little lids open and shut. She takes something for her blood pressure, and something for her cholesterol, and I think a water pill? But me, I’ve always been pretty lucky in the health department, physically speaking anyway. 

I haven't been to a regular doctor in... gosh, I don't even know how long. Years, probably. I mean, I'll take a Tylenol if I get a headache, or maybe one of those chalky antacids if I eat something too spicy, like when I tried that new chili recipe out of the magazine last month—which was a mistake, let me tell you. But as for actual prescriptions from a doctor? No, absolutely nothing. 

And I haven't started anything new either, not even those herbal supplements people are always talking about on the television. I see those commercials with the smiling older folks hiking up mountains and I think, well, maybe I should try whatever they're selling, but I never do. I just drink my water, try to eat my vegetables, and that’s about it. So, no, there aren't any pills or medications that could be causing this awful buzzing feeling, if that's what you're getting at. It's just me, all on my own, running like a motor for no good reason.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly describes feeling like they are 'running like a motor for no good reason,' which directly matches the symptom of acting as if driven by a motor.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond this feeling of restlessness, have you noticed that you've been feeling down, hopeless, or less interested in doing the things you usually enjoy lately?
turns.patient_response:
Well, gosh, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, I get terribly frustrated with myself, of course, because of all this pacing and not getting things done, but down? Hopeless? No, no. I'm actually a pretty cheerful person by nature, I really am. 

I know what that dark cloud feels like—I remember when my husband passed, God rest his soul, I had a spell where I was just so blue, wouldn't even open the living room curtains for weeks, you know how it is when grief just sits heavy on your chest. But that was years ago. Right now? I have all the interest in the world in doing things! Honestly, that's the whole tragedy of it all. 

Just last Tuesday, I bought this beautiful cross-stitch kit from the craft store over on Maple Street—it's a picture of a little chickadee sitting on a dogwood branch, just gorgeous, the kind of thing you'd frame and give as a nice gift. I was so excited to start it. I picked out all the little colored threads, got myself a brand new wooden hoop, set it all up by my favorite lamp... so the interest is absolutely there. I want to do it so badly! But I sit down with it, and five minutes later my legs are doing that buzzing thing, my mind is jumping over to whether I remembered to wipe down the baseboards in the guest bath, and suddenly I'm up walking around with the needle still in my hand. 

So it's certainly not that I don't care or don't want to do my hobbies. I just... I can't seem to settle down long enough to actually enjoy them. My neighbor Shirley, now she went through a real depression last winter and she wouldn't even get out of her pajamas or watch her favorite game shows, just completely lost her spark. But me? I'm dressed by seven in the morning, I've got a list of ten things I want to do in my head, I'm just... bouncing between them and not finishing a single one. So no, definitely not hopeless or depressed, just... well, just driving myself a little crazy, if I'm being perfectly honest!

turns.doctor_question: When you feel that 'buzzing' sensation and have to get up, do you also feel a sense of dread, apprehension, or a feeling that something bad is about to happen?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. Dread? Apprehension? No, it's not like that. It's not a scary feeling, like waiting for the other shoe to drop or thinking the house is going to catch fire. I know what you mean, though—my sister gets like that sometimes. She’ll call me up in a panic because she heard a siren three streets over and she’s just convinced it’s her grandson, even though he lives in Ohio. She gets that real tight feeling in her chest, you know, just waiting for bad news. 

But for me, it’s nothing like that. It’s not fear, and it’s certainly not dread. It’s just... physical, I guess? Like I said, it’s just this buzzing, this absolute need to move. When I’m sitting there trying to do my cross-stitch, or trying to watch the evening news—I like to watch the local broadcast at six, just to see what the weather’s going to do, though they’re wrong half the time anyway—I don’t feel like anything bad is going to happen. I just feel like if I don’t stand up and walk into the kitchen or the hallway right that very second, I’m going to jump right out of my own skin. 

It’s just antsy. Like a motor that won’t shut off. I’m not worried about the future or feeling like doom is around the corner. I’m just terribly, terribly restless. So, no, no dread at all. Just a lot of pacing!

turns.doctor_question: When you are sitting there and that motor starts running, do you find that your mind is racing with lots of different thoughts, or is your mind actually quite clear and focused on the fact that you just need to move?
turns.patient_response:
Well, gosh, it's definitely not clear. Clear is the last word I would use! It's more like... well, it's like my brain is a television set, and someone is just sitting there with the remote control, flipping through the channels as fast as they can go. Click, click, click, click. 

When I was trying to do that cross-stitch the other day, the chickadee one I told you about, I was sitting there, and the buzzing started in my legs, right? But my head was just as bad. I was looking at the yellow thread, and suddenly I'm thinking, "Oh, yellow, I need to buy lemons at the grocery store." And then, "Did I leave the coupon for the lemons on the kitchen counter?" And then, "I should really wipe down those counters, they get so dusty." And then, "I wonder if I should use that lemon-scented cleaner, or if the pine one is better for the grout." And before I know it, I'm thinking about the grout in the bathroom, and the fact that the shower curtain liner needs replacing, and whether I should get a clear one this time or a frosted one, because the frosted ones hide the water spots better...

It's just exhausting! It's never just one thought, and it's certainly never just the thought that I need to move. It's a whole parade of thoughts, all marching in at once, stepping all over each other. I'll be pacing the hallway, and I won't even remember why I stood up in the first place, because by the time I've taken three steps, my mind has already bounced from the lemons to the grout to the shower curtain to wondering if it's going to rain on Thursday. 

So no, my mind is definitely not clear. It's just as restless as my legs are, maybe even more so. It's like I have ten different trains of thought leaving the station at the exact same time, and I'm just running alongside them trying to catch one!

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your life, have you always felt this way, even when you were much younger, or is this something that has only started happening more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, my heavens, no, this isn't a new thing at all. Not even a little bit! If you asked anyone who knew me when I was a little girl, they’d tell you the exact same thing. 

I mean, I remember my mother—she kept all our old report cards in this beautiful cedar chest at the foot of her bed, the one with the brass handles, you know the kind?—and we were looking through them once years and years ago, and it was just the same story on every single piece of paper. Even back in grade school, my teachers wrote that I was bright, you know, a smart girl, but just so, so careless. 

I was always losing my papers. I’d do my homework at the kitchen table, I swear I would, and then just... poof! It would vanish before I got to school. Or it would turn up three weeks later crumpled into a ball at the very bottom of my bookbag underneath a squished permission slip. And the talking! Oh, I was always talking out of turn. Just blurting things out before the teacher even finished asking the question because the thought would pop into my head and it just had to come out right that second. 

And they were constantly, I mean constantly, needing to give me reminders to stay in my seat or to actually finish my work. I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade—she had these thick glasses and always wore these bright floral print dresses—she must have told me to sit down a dozen times a day. Because I’d do two arithmetic problems, and then I’d see a robin out the window, or I’d decide my pencil wasn't sharp enough, and suddenly I’m up and walking around the classroom visiting with the other children instead of finishing my worksheet. 

So, no, this isn't just something that came on recently in my old age. It’s been my whole life! I’ve always been a motor running too fast, always losing things, always bouncing around. You'd think by the time a person turns sixty-six they would have slowed down a bit, wouldn't you? You'd think the motor would run out of gas! But no, here I am, still pacing around my house and leaving half-finished cross-stitches everywhere, just exactly like I used to wander around Mrs. Gable's classroom. It's exhausting, really, just exhausting.
